title: Birth near Richmond, Virginia, and a catfish childhood
summary: Callender describes his conception in Boston, birth in Virginia, move to Atlantic City, and confirms his birth date and the family farm at Haynesville where he fished with his grandfather.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: ....[FIRST MINUTE NOT AUDIBLE]... For some reason, my mother went to Boston to work, I think, during that time, for a private family or something. And my father was a steward on a ship at that time. And they met. And so, I was conceived in Boston, but afterwards they married, of course -- they had to be very up to par. Anyway, my mother went to Virginia and I had me, and two months later they took me back to Boston, and after that back to Virginia. I remember staying in Virginia until I was about 3, and then we moved to Atlantic City. My memory is excellent...

Yes, we went to Atlantic City, and when I was 5, I went into the First Grade -- skipped the kindergarten. So I was always the youngest one. Even in later years, when I started playing in bands, I was the youngest one. But now that's changed completely! [LAUGHS]
To go back to the beginning: Is the birth-date that is in all these reference books the correct one?
March 6, 1918. [IN Unfinished Dream: The Musical World of Red Callender, HE CITES MARCH 6, 1916]
I want to confirm that one. And it was Richmond, Virginia.

Richmond, Virginia. Yes, that's where I was born. Not actually in Richmond; Richmond is a city. But my folks had a farm outside of Richmond, and actually it was called Haynesville, Post Office. I remember that. There was a screen through the back, which is not important to this, but anyhow I can remember it. I used to go back there and fish with my grandfather, who would take a bent pin and put a worm on it, and go back in the stream and fish -- he'd catch catfish. I remember being a little guy, I got stuck in a thing...those things that come out of the catfish...
I never caught a catfish... Yes, I think I did, come to think of it.
Well, if you've seen a catfish, then you know those...

They look like whiskers. But anyhow, I got stuck with one, and I've been pretty shy ever since. So years later, when I took my family fishing, I used to put gloves on. They'd laugh at me. I'd put rubber gloves on. So finally I got so I could touch a worm again. Which has nothing to do with music, but all that happened.
Well, no, this is your life, and your life in music -- it's all of your life that you want to talk
